title: Operating System
body:
The program that owns the machine and rents it out to yours. It appears at the end of this
course as the answer to a question the hardware keeps raising: the [[CPU]] does not know
which addresses are protected, does not know which program should run next, and does not
know what a file is. Something has to, and that something is the OS.

Two jobs, and they pull in opposite directions:

- **Abstraction.** Turn the machine into something usable. Files instead of disk sectors,
  processes instead of a single [[Motorola 68000]], a byte stream instead of the
  [[6850 ACIA]]'s registers.
- **Arbitration.** Decide who gets the [[CPU]], the memory, and the devices, and stop
  programs interfering with each other.

Both need privilege, which is why the [[Kernel]] runs in [[Supervisor State]] and why a
[[System Call]] is the only way in. The errors this course teaches are mostly the OS
noticing: a bus error is an access to an address it protected, a privilege violation is a
program trying to skip the doorway. See [[Assembly Errors]].

On the Atari ST used in this course the OS is TOS: GEMDOS for files and processes, BIOS and
XBIOS for the hardware, GEM for the windowing. All reached by `trap`.

[[OPERATING SYSTEMS]] takes it from here and spends a whole course on scheduling
([[Processes]], [[CPU Scheduling]]), memory ([[Virtual Memory]]), and coordination
([[Synchronization]]).
